strengths: Clear and well-motivated engineering contribution: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to bring multi-token prediction to structured language models for 3D perception, and it carefully identifies the two failure modes of naive MTP (accuracy degradation and parameter overhead) before addressing them.

Strong and convincing empirical results. On ASE, Fast SceneScript (SSD, n=10) achieves a 5.09x latency reduction over SceneScript (382 ms to 75 ms) while slightly improving mean F1 (0.912 vs 0.913 val, 0.912 vs 0.915 test); similar gains hold on Structured3D (5.57x faster with +2.07% F1). Compared to the naive MTP baseline, it delivers substantially better accuracy (e.g., 0.912 vs 0.840 mean F1 with 8 heads on ASE) with ~43% fewer parameters.

The ablation study (Table 3) is thorough and supports each design choice separately: the distance tolerance for numerical tokens (tau = 0 vs 2 vs 5), the head-sharing parameter-efficient mechanism (w/o sharing rows), and the scoring-based alternatives (ProductThre, SoftmaxThre vs. the proposed CGD).

The qualitative analysis (Figs. 7 and 8) is a nice addition: the distribution analysis showing that softmax confidence does not correlate well with actual token reliability directly motivates CGD and is an insightful observation beyond the immediate benchmark numbers.

Comparison to a strong task-specific baseline (RoomFormer) on Structured3D shows the method outperforms it in F1 with fewer decoder parameters, contextualizing the results beyond the SceneScript family.

The paper is generally well written, with clear motivation (the predictability of structured language vs. natural language justifying MTP), a clean framework figure (Fig. 3), and adequate implementation details (decoder architecture, optimizer, loss weights, tau, epochs) for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components. MTP follows [12], SSD follows [32, 51] with a distance-metric tolerance for numerical tokens (Eq. 3) as a modest adaptation, and CGD's confidence heads trained against first-head agreement are closely related to Medusa-style confidence mechanisms [4] and scoring-based thresholding [21, 37]. The parameter-efficient mechanism is essentially weight sharing across heads plus a lightweight FFN projection block. The contribution is a well-executed combination rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Evaluation breadth is narrow relative to the claims of generality. The introduction and related work position SceneScript as a generalist model for layout estimation, 3D object detection, and 3D part reconstruction, but all experiments are on layout estimation (wall/window/door classes) only. The claim that Fast SceneScript 'provides a general framework with potential applications to other 3D perception tasks' is untested.

The headline '12.04% improvement in F1-Score' in Fig. 1 is measured against the weak naive-MTP baseline (SceneScript + MTP), not against the state of the art; against vanilla SceneScript the accuracy is essentially matched rather than improved on ASE. The framing slightly overstates the accuracy contribution.

Some methodological questions are underexplored. The tolerance-based acceptance (tau = 2) for numerical tokens effectively allows small geometric discrepancies, but the paper does not analyze how the geometric quantization of numerical tokens relates to tau (i.e., what physical distance tolerance tau=2 implies), nor whether accepted-but-perturbed coordinates degrade downstream geometric metrics in ways the 5cm-bucketed F1 may mask. CGD's confidence targets are derived from train-time head agreement; a discussion of whether these confidences generalize under distribution shift is missing.

Minor clarity/consistency issues: the explanation of the loss weight lambda_h is contradictory (text says later heads are more uncertain and 'incur a higher loss' while also describing lambda_h as a decaying factor); Table 2 contains typographical corruption ('20 91 M'); 'Additionly' in Fig. 1; 'We employ' capitalization mid-sentence. No code release is mentioned, which somewhat limits reproducibility for a systems/efficiency paper.

Scalability is unexamined: results are limited to a small decoder (8 layers, dim 512) and n in {8, 10}, with the observation that larger n degrades performance relegated to supplementary material. It is unclear how the approach behaves on larger decoder capacities, which would strengthen the generality claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and relevant problem: autoregressive decoding is a well-known latency bottleneck for language-based perception models such as SceneScript, and the reported 5.09x (ASE) and 4.58-5.57x (Structured3D) speedups with parity-level F1-Score represent a meaningful practical improvement.

The experimental evaluation is reasonably thorough: two benchmarks (ASE, Structured3D), both val and test splits on ASE, a baseline re-implementation (Row b) in addition to the author-released model (Row a), and a dedicated ablation (Tab. 3) covering the distance threshold tau, the head-sharing mechanism, and two alternative scoring strategies (ProductThre, SoftmaxThre).

The comparison against the naive SceneScript + MTP baseline is informative and directly demonstrates the failure mode the paper aims to fix: plain MTP with 8/10 heads degrades mean F1 by ~7-11% while inflating decoder parameters by 69-89%, whereas Fast SceneScript maintains accuracy with ~15-16M parameters.

The analysis of why softmax-based scoring fails (Fig. 8: accepted tokens with low softmax confidence, rejected tokens with high confidence) provides a useful empirical insight supporting the proposed CGD scoring, and the accepted-token distributions in Fig. 7 are a nice diagnostic.

The writing and figures (framework in Fig. 3, decoding strategies in Fig. 4) are generally clear and the method components are described at a level that supports reproducibility (architecture, loss weights, thresholds, optimizer settings, hardware for latency).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients are established techniques. Multi-token prediction is from [12]/DeepSeek-V3, self-speculative decoding is Draft&Verify-style [32, 51], and CGD is essentially a Medusa-style [4] self-consistency/confidence head adapted to this setting. The parameter-efficient mechanism (shared heads plus a two-layer FFN projection block) is a straightforward design. The contribution is primarily an application/adaptation of known inference-acceleration machinery to one specific perception model (SceneScript), which weakens the case for a top-tier contribution.

Headline claims are somewhat inflated by framing: the advertised '12.04% higher F1-Score' (Fig. 1, abstract) is measured against SceneScript + MTP, i.e., a strawman baseline, not against SceneScript itself. Compared to the properly trained SceneScript (Row b), Fast SceneScript is approximately at parity (0.912 vs 0.913 val; 0.912 vs 0.915 test on ASE), so the accuracy story is 'no regression,' not 'improvement.' This framing should be stated more honestly.

Generality of the framework is asserted but not demonstrated. The 'general framework with potential applications to other 3D perception tasks' claim (object detection, part reconstruction) is unsupported by any experiment; the paper is validated only on wall/window/door layout estimation. A result on even one additional structured-output task would substantially strengthen the contribution.

Some methodological subtleties are under-justified. (i) In SSD, verification tokens are generated conditioned on unverified draft prefixes; the interaction between the distance tolerance tau=2 for numerical tokens and downstream autoregressive drift is not analyzed (e.g., whether small accepted coordinate errors propagate). (ii) CGD confidences cover only heads 2..n, with the claim that head 1 is 'typically more reliable' offered without evidence. (iii) The CGD ground-truth confidence is defined relative to the first head's output rather than ground truth, which conflates 'consistent with head 1' and 'correct'; the F1 numbers suggest this works in practice, but the reasoning is circular.

The efficiency comparison could be broader. Alternatives such as simply using a smaller decoder, KV-cache optimizations, or quantization are not discussed as competing speedup routes, making it hard to judge whether MTP is the best use of engineering effort for this model; the RoomFormer comparison in Tab. 2 (54 ms vs 211-257 ms) shows non-AR structured approaches remain far faster, with the paper's argument resting on generality rather than measured versatility.

Evaluation scope is narrow on the task side (three classes: wall, window, door) and the latency benefit depends on sequence length; ASE shows a large gap (387 ms baseline) but the Structured3D training set is very small (3,000 scenes, 600 epochs initialized from ASE), raising questions about variance and robustness that are not addressed with error bars or repeated runs.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: autoregressive next-token decoding is the dominant latency bottleneck in language-based perception models such as SceneScript, and the paper clearly frames why structured perception languages (predictable, deterministic token sequences) are a good fit for multi-token prediction.

The proposed solution is well-rounded: it combines (1) MTP with decaying loss weights, (2) two complementary token-filtering strategies — adapted self-speculative decoding with a distance metric for numerical tokens (Eq. 3), and the new confidence-guided decoding (CGD) with learned confidence heads — and (3) a parameter-efficient head-sharing mechanism with a lightweight projection block. Each component is clearly motivated and described in enough detail to reproduce.

The empirical evidence is extensive and convincing. Tables 1 and 2 cover two datasets (ASE, Structured3D), multiple head counts (n=4,6,8,10), and report accuracy (F1), latency, parameter count, and average accepted tokens (α). The headline results — 5.09× speedup on ASE and 5.57× on Structured3D with comparable or better F1, and ~7.5% parameter overhead — are well supported by the reported numbers (e.g., Row i vs Row b in both tables).

The ablation study (Table 3) is thorough: it isolates the effect of the numerical distance threshold τ (rows c–e), validates the head-sharing mechanism against the full-head variant (rows d/f, i/j, showing ~48% fewer parameters without accuracy loss), and compares CGD against two established scoring-based strategies (ProductThre, SoftmaxThre), with the token-acceptance distributions in Fig. 7 and softmax-score analysis in Fig. 8 providing insightful evidence that softmax confidence is a poor proxy for token reliability in this setting.

The comparison against the naive SceneScript+MTP baseline is a valuable negative result: it quantifies the accuracy degradation (up to 11% F1 drop) and parameter bloat (~89% increase at n=10) of naively applying MTP, which strengthens the case for the proposed filtering and parameter-efficiency contributions.
The paper is honest about limitations, e.g., acknowledging that RoomFormer is faster in absolute latency (54 ms vs 230 ms) while noting Fast SceneScript's generality advantage.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: MTP, self-speculative decoding, and scoring-based token filtering all exist in the LLM literature (Medusa, Draft&Verify, Dynamo, etc.), and the core contributions are adaptations of these techniques to structured perception language models. The distance metric for numerical tokens (Eq. 3) and the confidence-head design are sensible but relatively straightforward extensions. The paper's positioning as 'first MTP for language-based perception models' is a fair claim, but the methodological contribution is incremental.

The claimed 12.04% F1 improvement (Fig. 1, abstract) is relative to the weak SceneScript+MTP baseline, not to the original SceneScript. Against SceneScript itself, Fast SceneScript is essentially accuracy-neutral on ASE (0.913 vs 0.912/0.913 mean F1) — the real gain is speed. This framing could be more candid, as the abstract may mislead a casual reader into expecting an accuracy contribution.

Task and evaluation breadth is limited to 3D layout estimation with three primitive classes (wall, window, door). The paper motivates the work via generalist perception (object detection, part reconstruction), but no experiments demonstrate that the approach transfers to those tasks, leaving the generality claim unverified.

Some methodological questions remain insufficiently analyzed: (1) CGD's confidence ground truth is defined by agreement between MTP heads rather than by correctness against the actual ground truth, so the learned 'confidence' measures self-consistency — the paper does not analyze when this proxy could fail (e.g., systematically wrong but self-consistent predictions); (2) the tolerance τ=2 for numerical tokens (in token units, presumably cm/bin) relaxes exactness of coordinates, and while F1 at 5cm granularity is unaffected, the effect on downstream geometric precision is not examined.

Latency is measured only on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, a consumer GPU; results on more representative inference hardware, or a breakdown of the verification-pass overhead for SSD (which needs a second forward pass) versus CGD, would strengthen the efficiency claims. The reason CGD is slower than SSD on Structured3D (269 ms vs 230 ms at n=8) despite avoiding verification is not analyzed.

The improvement over the NTP baseline in F1 on Structured3D (0.791 vs 0.774) is attributed to the method, but it is not clearly dissected whether this stems from the filtering, the training schedule (600 epochs, ASE initialization), or regularization effects of MTP — a control experiment isolating this would help.
No statement about code release is provided, which limits reproducibility given the many hyperparameters (λh, λc, τ, thresholds for baseline scoring methods).

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing experimental evaluation: results are reported on three datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD) spanning synthetic and real-world data, across two tasks (layout estimation and 3D object detection), with extensive ablations in both main paper and supplementary material covering thresholds (τ, ε), head counts (n=4 to 16), supervision strategies for the confidence branch, and the effect of the parameter-sharing mechanism.

The core claims are well supported by the tables: Fast SceneScript (SSD) achieves ~5.09× speedup with essentially unchanged F1-Score (0.912 vs 0.913 on ASE val), while plain MTP degrades accuracy substantially (e.g., 0.815 vs 0.915 with 10 heads), validating the central premise that token filtering is necessary to make MTP viable for structured perception languages.

The parameter-efficient head-sharing mechanism is clearly effective: Tables 4 (rows i vs j) and S1 show 48–55% fewer decoder parameters with no accuracy loss, and Fig. 1's parameter comparison against MTP-n is compelling.

The paper is well written and well organized; the motivation that structured perception languages are more deterministic and weakly coupled than natural language, making multi-token prediction more tractable, is a useful insight that could generalize to other sequence-based perception models (Pix2Seq-style, SpatialLM).

The empirical analysis of why softmax-based scoring fails (Figs. 6, 7, S2–S4) — showing tokens accepted/rejected inconsistently with softmax confidence — is a valuable contribution beyond just reporting final metrics.

Honest reporting: the paper includes the author-released baseline comparison, notes where RoomFormer is faster for the layout-only task, and provides failure cases and a longer-training control (Tab. S5) that rules out undertrained baselines.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: the paper primarily adapts existing techniques from the LLM literature (multi-token prediction [14], self-speculative decoding [35,54], Medusa-style auxiliary heads, scoring-based filtering [23,40]) to a new domain. The technical novelties — a distance-based acceptance criterion for numerical tokens and a learned confidence head (CGD, which resembles Medusa's typical-acceptance scheme) — are sensible but incremental.

The proposed CGD is trained to predict agreement with the first head's output, so its advantage over simply using the first head's softmax probability (thresholded) is not fully disentangled from the choice of threshold; the comparison to ProductThre/SoftmaxThre in Tab. 4 uses thresholds tuned 'for efficiency–accuracy trade-offs', and a more careful threshold-sensitivity comparison (partially covered in Tab. S2) would strengthen the claim that CGD is fundamentally better.

Object detection evaluation on ASE relies on pseudo-ground-truth boxes generated by TR3D rather than real annotations, which adds label noise and weakens the strength of the detection conclusions; the F1@.50 gap versus SceneScript (0.829 vs 0.823) is small relative to this noise source.

SSD requires a second decoder forward pass for verification, meaning the effective compute per accepted token is not directly comparable to the single-pass CGD variants; the paper reports wall-clock latency but does not decompose FLOPs or discuss the trade-off in terms of total compute.

Evaluation breadth is somewhat narrow: only indoor scene tasks with a single underlying architecture (SceneScript) are tested; the generality of the approach to other structured-language perception models (e.g., Pix2Seq, SpatialLM) remains unverified, making the 'first work to introduce MTP to language-based perception models' claim meaningful but its broader significance uncertain.

Some methodological details are under-specified in the main text: τ=2 is stated without units or justification of scale relative to the token vocabulary/quantization scheme; the role and weighting of the decaying loss factor λ_h is deferred to following prior work.

Several reported gains over the strongest baselines are modest (e.g., CGD slightly faster than SSD but slightly lower accuracy; SceneCAD improvements partly confounded by the small 1k-scene training set), so the practical impact rests mainly on the speed–accuracy–parameter trade-off rather than accuracy improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practical bottleneck: autoregressive next-token decoding is the dominant latency cost in language-based perception models like SceneScript, and the proposed solution yields substantial speedups (5.09x on layout estimation, 5.14x on object detection) while matching the accuracy of the NTP baseline (e.g., Tab. 1: Fast SceneScript SSD mean F1 0.912/0.913 vs. SceneScript 0.913/0.915).

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: three datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD), two tasks (layout estimation and 3D object detection), two decoding strategies (SSD and CGD), and a fairly thorough set of ablations (Tab. 4, S1-S4) covering threshold sensitivity, head counts from 8 to 16, head-sharing vs. separate heads, confidence supervision strategies, and softmax-score distribution analyses (Figs. 6, 7, S2, S4).

The proposed CGD decoding is a sensible alternative to SSD: it avoids the one-step verification delay by training confidence heads to predict inter-head consistency, and the comparison against ProductThre/SoftmaxThre baselines (Tab. 4 rows g-j, Fig. 6) supports the claim that softmax-based scores are poor proxies for token reliability in structured languages.

The evaluation is mostly honest: the paper retrained the SceneScript baseline (Row b, Tab. 1) rather than relying on the released model, reports both SSD and CGD even where CGD is slower (e.g., Structured3D: 269 ms vs. 230 ms), includes failure cases (Fig. S5), and ablates the baseline with longer training (Tab. S5).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core ingredients are all established techniques: multi-token prediction [14], self-speculative decoding [35, 54], and scoring-based filtering [23, 40]. The adaptations are incremental: (i) a distance tolerance tau for numerical tokens (Eq. 3, essentially a small design tweak), (ii) a confidence head predicting inter-head agreement, and (iii) a shared-head/projection-block design that is a straightforward parameter-sharing scheme. The paper reads as a well-executed engineering adaptation of known inference-acceleration methods to a specific model, rather than a new method or insight.

The headline '12.04% F1-Score improvement' (Fig. 1, abstract-adjacent claims) is measured against the paper's own degraded SceneScript+MTP baseline (Row h, Tab. 1), not against SceneScript itself. Against the actual NTP baseline, Fast SceneScript achieves essentially parity (0.912 vs. 0.913 on ASE val), so the accuracy claim reduces to 'no degradation', which is the expected outcome given lossless-style token filtering. Framing this as an accuracy contribution is overstated.

Object detection evaluation relies on pseudo-labels: bounding-box annotations for ASE are generated by TR3D predictions rather than ground truth (Sec. 4.1), introducing label noise of unknown magnitude. Both the baseline and the proposed method are trained on these noisy labels, so F1@0.25/0.5 comparisons may not reflect true detection quality, and no analysis of this noise is provided.

CGD's claimed advantage of 'on-the-fly' decoding does not consistently translate into lower latency: it is slower than SSD in most reported settings (92 ms vs. 81 ms on ASE n=8; 269 ms vs. 230 ms on Structured3D; 108 ms vs. 104 ms on detection), and the trade-off between the two strategies is discussed only qualitatively. The practical value of CGD relative to simply using SSD remains unclear.

Results appear to be from single training runs with no variance or statistical significance reported, despite small accuracy differences (e.g., 0.912 vs. 0.913 F1) being used to support claims such as 'MTP acts as a beneficial regularizer'.

The claimed parameter reduction (~43%) is relative to the paper's own naive MTP baseline with separate heads, not to the field; and the head-sharing mechanism itself is not rigorously justified beyond intuition ('shared semantic space'), with limited analysis of when sharing might fail.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned, and latency numbers are hardware-dependent (RTX 2080 Ti). The dataset split files and hyperparameters in the supplementary help, but independent verification would be difficult.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the observation that structured languages for visual perception are more deterministic than natural language makes MTP a natural fit, and the paper is the first to bring multi-token prediction to language-based perception models like SceneScript.

Comprehensive experimental support: results on three datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD), two tasks (layout estimation and 3D object detection), systematic comparison against both NTP and naive MTP baselines, plus substantial ablations in the supplementary material (number of heads, thresholds, supervision strategies, architecture details).

Both proposed filtering strategies are meaningfully compared: SSD offers higher throughput (α≈8-9 accepted tokens) while CGD offers on-the-fly decoding; the trade-off analysis is transparent rather than cherry-picked (Tables 1-5).

The parameter-efficient head-sharing mechanism is well supported by ablations: Rows d/f and i/j in Table 4 show shared heads reduce parameters by ~43-48% with negligible accuracy loss, and the design rationale (position-dependent hidden states in a shared semantic space) is plausible.

The analysis in Figs. 6-7 and S2-S4 is a nice touch, demonstrating quantitatively that softmax scores are poor proxies for token reliability in this setting and motivating CGD, and the supplementary analyses (confidence supervision strategies, longer-training baseline control in Tab. S5) show unusual diligence.

Strong and consistent empirical results: ~5.09×/5.14× speedup on layout estimation and object detection with essentially no accuracy loss, and large gains over naive SceneScript+MTP (+12.04% F1 with 43% fewer parameters), on both synthetic and real-world data.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental: MTP (Gloeckle et al., DeepSeek-V3), self-speculative decoding (Stern et al., Draft&Verify), and scoring-based filtering (ProductThre, SoftmaxThre) are all established; the genuinely new pieces are (a) the distance-based acceptance criterion for numerical tokens, (b) the CGD confidence head, and (c) shared heads. Each is sensible but individually simple.

CGD's confidence supervision is heuristic: ground-truth labels are derived from consistency with the first head's output rather than actual correctness. The GT-supervision ablation (Tab. S4) shows comparable accuracy but higher α for the consistency-based variant; the argument that 'internal disagreement models uncertainty' is asserted rather than rigorously analyzed.

The SSD variant with distance tolerance τ is lossy decoding: accepting numerical tokens that differ by up to τ=2 coordinates could accumulate geometric error, particularly for long token sequences; the paper does not analyze error accumulation or per-coordinate distribution of accepted/rejected numerical tokens.

Speed comparisons are somewhat favorable to the proposed method: raw latency of Fast SceneScript (e.g., 81-92 ms on ASE, 230-269 ms on Structured3D) is slower than the naive SceneScript+MTP variants (62 ms, 171 ms); the headline 5.09× speedup is always measured against the NTP baseline. The efficiency-accuracy framing is honest, but the headline claim could be stated more carefully.

Real-world evaluation is thin: SceneCAD results are reported only on the val set (~1k training scenes), and ASE object detection relies on pseudo-ground-truth boxes generated by TR3D rather than human annotations, which conflates detector errors with model errors. There is no evaluation on Omni3D or other established real-world 3D detection benchmarks.
No explicit statement about code release, which would affect reproducibility of the CGD training pipeline and the relatively intricate decoding logic.

Minor presentation issues: some notation is inconsistent between main paper and supplement (head-index omission acknowledged in footnote), and several sentences contain grammatical errors (e.g., 'spawn', 'a simple and end-to-end manner').
